# True or false: Quality

Quality is built in while the code is written, not inspected at the end. These statements check what you believe about testers, TDD and test suites.

10 statements (Foundation 4, Standard 5, Assured 1). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area quality`.

### 1. Quality is best assured by a separate QA team that tests after development is finished.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Testing at the end turns QA into a queue, releases slip, and defects still escape. Make quality the whole team's job while the code is written. Testers become quality engineers who coach, automate and explore.

Read more: [playbook/quality/quality-engineering.md](../../playbook/quality/quality-engineering.md)

</details>

### 2. The number of test cases executed before a release is a good measure of quality.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Running more test cases measures effort, not what users experience. Measure escaped defects, change fail rate and recovery time instead. These show whether quality reached production.

Read more: [playbook/quality/quality-engineering.md](../../playbook/quality/quality-engineering.md)

</details>

### 3. Human testers add the most value through exploratory testing, not by re-running scripted manual checks.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Stable, repeatable checks are cheaper and faster when automated. People are better at finding what nobody thought to script. Automate the stable checks and spend human time exploring.

Read more: [playbook/quality/quality-engineering.md](../../playbook/quality/quality-engineering.md)

</details>

### 4. TDD should be mandated for all code and checked by looking at commit order.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Use TDD where mistakes are expensive and the expected behaviour can be stated up front, such as pricing or permission rules. Policing commit order rewards the ritual, not the result. Judge it by test quality and escaped defects.

Read more: [playbook/quality/test-driven-development.md](../../playbook/quality/test-driven-development.md)

</details>

### 5. Refactoring is a required step of the TDD cycle, not an optional extra.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** TDD works in short cycles of test, code and refactor. Skip the refactor and the design never improves, even though the tests pass. The passing tests are what make the refactor safe.

Read more: [playbook/quality/test-driven-development.md](../../playbook/quality/test-driven-development.md)

</details>

### 6. Good unit tests mock every collaborator and assert the order of calls.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Tests like this check how the code is written, so they break on every refactor and miss real behaviour. Test what the code observably does. Use real objects inside the module boundary and real dependencies in containers for integration tests.

Read more: [playbook/quality/test-driven-development.md](../../playbook/quality/test-driven-development.md)

</details>

### 7. Tests written after the code tend to confirm what the code already does, rather than what it should do.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** When the code exists first, it is natural to write tests that match it. Cases the author did not think of stay untested. Writing the failing test from the requirement first avoids that.

Read more: [playbook/quality/test-driven-development.md](../../playbook/quality/test-driven-development.md)

</details>

### 8. Many fast unit and component tests plus a few end-to-end tests give quicker and more reliable feedback than hundreds of end-to-end tests.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Hundreds of end-to-end tests are slow and flaky, and they take an hour to tell you little. Push checks down to unit, component and contract tests. Keep 5 to 20 end-to-end tests for the critical paths.

Read more: [playbook/delivery/testing.md](../../playbook/delivery/testing.md)

</details>

### 9. Mutation testing can reveal weak tests even when coverage numbers look good.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Mutation testing changes the code on purpose and checks whether any test fails. If the tests still pass, they run the code without really checking it. Use it on critical modules such as pricing, permissions and tax rules.

Read more: [playbook/delivery/testing.md](../../playbook/delivery/testing.md)

</details>

### 10. In TDD, if you have been stuck without a passing test for about 10 minutes, it is often better to revert and take a smaller step.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Being stuck usually means the step was too large. Reverting to the last green state costs little and gives a clean start. Write a smaller test and continue from there.

Read more: [playbook/quality/test-driven-development.md](../../playbook/quality/test-driven-development.md)

</details>
